#1425. Scotland’s Pocognoli era starts with encouraging signs but familiar issues in front of goal

Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb

“It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play,” McBurnie told BBC Scotland.

“We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored. I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

“Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”

However, the goal that would have made the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager’s debut as an international boss more memorable ultimately failed to arrive.

In this extended international break, the Scots will host Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday and then travel to North Macedonia before taking on Slovenia in Glasgow, with the Tartan Army hoping to see further improvement – and goals.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, the debutant said: “Thought we struggled to get into the game first half, but second half we completely dominated the game.

“They’ve got a top goalie who made really good saves. So many positives to take and a clean sheet as well.

“We changed shape a wee bit at half-time to get more control and that did really well for us.

“It’s a big game again on Tuesday so it’s important to recover now and go again.

“I’ve played on the left-hand side for a couple of years now, so I’m comfortable doing that.

“We’ve had a great week. A new manager, new way of playing and new faces in camp. It’s just the chances we need to take - the fact we’re creating the chances stands us in good stead.”

The striker told BBC Scotland: “It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play.

“We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored.

“I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

“Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”

Pocognoli’s first game in charge of Scotland ends in a goalless draw. The visitors produced a dominant second-half display, but their final ball and end-product was severely lacking in crucial moments. Ure, Hickey, Gilmour, McBurnie and Bowie all came close to scoring, but no one could break the deadlock.

Scotland cannot find a way past the impenetrable Oblak. There will be just two minutes of added time for the visitors to possibly score a late winner.

Lovric clatters into Gilmour and is cautioned. Slovenia can’t get out. It’s wave after wave of Scottish pressure.

Oblak comes out and fails to claim Robertson’s free-kick. The ball is recycled and the Tottenham full-back whips a second cross into the box and Slovenia fail to clear. Welsh is waiting for it, but lashes a first-time volley over the bar.

Karnicnik catches Robertson with a late lunging tackle and receives a yellow card, giving Scotland a chance to get the ball into the box.

The hosts make their fifth alteration of the afternoon, with Cerin withdrawn and Lovric on instead.

How has Bowie missed?! Gilmour finds Bowie with an outstanding pass through the centre of Slovenia’s defence. The substitute takes a touch then scuffs a rushed finish wide. Bowie has to do better there!

Another change is here for Scotland, with Gannon-Doak on to replace Hickey.

Another big chance for Scotland. This time Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie goes close.Slovenia 0-0 Scotland - watch the closing stages on BBC One. pic.twitter.com/xMe5gRNgEr

From the resulting corner, Oblak is there again to thwart McBurnie’s point-blank header. The referee then blows his whistle to relieve the pressure on Slovenia. Somehow, the scoreline remains goalless.

The hosts make another double change as Sporar and Brekalo depart for Vipotnik and Balkovec.

Welsh spots Bowie’s run and threads a perfectly-weighted pass through to the forward. From an unfavourable angle, the substitute’s one-on-one attempt is blocked by Oblak.

Another massive chance for Scotland! McGinn’s searching corner is met by Hickey, who flicks a header wide of the far post. Scotland’s second-half performance deserves a goal.

Pocognoli orders Scotland’s first alteration of the game, with Bowie replacing Ure up top.

Hickey finds himself very high up the pitch and tries to tee up Ure with a cushioned header, but there isn’t enough power on the pass.

Gilmour and Ure link up effectively on the counter, but the latter’s pull-back is intercepted by Drkusic.

Slovenia then make two changes as Zabukovnik and Zec replace Elsnik and Drkusic.

McGinn strides forward and tries to find Ure, but Slovenia rush back to scramble it clear. Scotland are really pushing for the opening goal.

Gilmour and McBurnie play a devastating one-two, allowing the midfielder to advance into the penalty area. He shoots and aims for the far corner, but his placed effort is collected impressively by Oblak, who makes another crucial intervention.

The second half has started as the first ended, with Scotland applying all of the pressure. Slovenia have Oblak to thank for the goalless scoreline.

McBurnie and Oblak both challenge for the ball, with the Scotsman bumping into the goalkeeper, giving Slovenia a goal kick. The decision is met by a chorus of boos from the away fans.

McBurnie latches onto a loose ball and skips away from Drkusic’s sliding challenge. One-on-one, the striker tries to round Oblak, but the Slovenian goalkeeper does sensationally to apprehend him. Upon reflection, it looks like McBurnie should have just shot and tried to put the ball between Oblak’s legs. He did the hard part, but lacked a clinical finish.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb

McGinn brilliantly turns Drkusic on the halfway line and then tees up Gilmour. The Napoli midfielder tries to float a pass over to the onrushing Robertson, but he hits the switch of play straight out for a throw-in. In defence of Gilmour, the pitch really doesn’t look in the best condition, with various players struggling regarding their weight of pass.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Pocognoli’s Scotland finished the half as the better side, but an opening goal has proved to be elusive. At times, they’ve looked suspect defensively and have lacked rhythm going forward. However, Pocognoli’s squad have only been together for a few days and are playing in a new system. Can they produce a more inspired second-half performance?

Despite Scotland’s late push for an opening goal at the end of the first half, the two sides head in level at the break. Slovenia started on the front-foot, with Sporar and Drkusic both going close for the hosts, before Ure struck the post to be denied a dream debut goal.

HALF TIME: Slovenia 0-0 Scotland.No goals at the break in Ljubljana.#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/6VGFRprBiz

Ure strikes the woodwork! The Sevilla striker is agonisingly close to a debut goal for his country. He cuts inside to work some space and fires a low effort at goal, but his shot hits the post.

Scotland's best chance of the game so far 😯 Sevilla striker and debutant Robbie Ure strikes the post just before half-time.However, it remains goalless at the break.📺 Watch Slovenia v Scotland on BBC One 🇸🇮 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 pic.twitter.com/fm1wH2fOej

Much better from Scotland! McGinn turns his marker and clips a wonderful pass over to Ure, who has drifted out wide. The ball is then delivered into the box toward McGinn, whose header bounces off McBurnie. Hickey is arriving to pounce on the loose ball, but the wing-back’s effort is blocked by the Slovenian defence.

Robertson picks up the game’s first yellow card for an off-the-ball incident. The Scotland captain is clearly very unhappy with the decision as we await to see a replay. Nevertheless, the action resumes with a Slovenia free-kick.

Slovenia go close again as a corner is whipped in. Drkusic wins the header at the near post and it bounces off the outside of the near post. That is definitely another warning sign for Scotland.

Matko goes on the outside of Welsh, and from a tight angle, he shoots, but his fizzed effort saves the side netting of the near post. Some fans behind the goal cheer because they think it’s gone in, but their view has really deceived them.

It’s been a quiet afternoon for both goalkeepers so far, with neither yet to make a noteworthy save. On a couple of occasions, Slovenia have had encouraging opportunities to get the ball into the Scotland’s box, but the deliveries have been overhit and poorly executed.

Similarly to Scotland, Slovenia are also playing a tremendously high-line. Unlike Slovenia, Scotland have been unable to find the right pass in behind the home side’s defence. Gilmour then carelessly gives the ball away as Scotland’s latest spell of possession ends.

Since Slovenia wasted that 14th-minute chance, Scotland have grown into the contest and are beginning to look comfortable in possession. However, they’re still waiting to craft their first notable opening here.

The hosts miss a huge chance! Once again, Sturm gets in behind Scotland’s incredibly high line and then fires a low cross into the penalty area. Sporar then beats McKenna to the delivery, but taps his close-range effort wide of the far post from inside the six-yard box. That’s a massive let-off for Scotland...

Matko is unleashed by a drilled pass then pierces through a gap between Robertson and Welsh. The Slovenia winger drives into the penalty area and tries to find either Sturm or Sporar with a cross, but Hendry does magnificently to make a last-ditch clearance.

Slovenia have the ball in the net, but the offside flag is up. Sturm gets in behind Scotland’s defence and slides a low cross into Sporar’s path. The striker then sweeps a composed first-time effort into the top corner. It’s a brilliant finish, but Sturm was miles offside in the build-up.

Gunn comes out confidently to collect a looping cross, before the ball is launched forward in McBurnie’s direction. The Hull City striker and Ure are playing really close to each other, very much like an old-school front-two.

Slovenia forward Sturm is wiped out by Hendry’s wild early challenge. The Scotland defender is perhaps lucky to avoid a booking. Welsh then heads the resulting set-piece away and out for a corner.

The hosts get us underway in the Slovenian capital. Can Pocognoli begin his Scotland tenure with a Nations League victory?

Both teams are out on the pitch in Ljubljana. We are moments away from the start of the Pocognoli era.

New Scotland manager Sebastien Pocognoli sings Flower of Scotland as he takes charge of the national side for the first time 🎶 🇸🇮 Slovenia v Scotland 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 is live on BBC One now.#BBCFootball #NationsLeague pic.twitter.com/I2aeqYkNGB

With just over 10 minutes until kick-off, here’s a reminder of both teams’ line-ups.

Slovenia: Oblak, Brekalo, Bijol, Drkusic, Janza, Karnicnik, Cerin, Elsnik, Matko, Sturm, Sporar.

Subs: Vidovsek, Leban, Balkovec, Zabukovnik, Kuzmic, Begic, Lovric, Celar, Svetlin, Zec, Vipotnik, Horvat.

Scotland: Gunn, Hendry, McKenna, Welsh, Hickey, Gilmour, Ferguson, Robertson, McGinn, Ure, McBurnie.

Subs: Kelly, Bain, Binks, Doig, Christie, Miller, McPake, Doak, Graham, Bowie, Patterson, Montgomery.

"Let's go!" 👏#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/HBvPJdFkFb

Luis Binks of Brondby, as well as Colby Donovan and Josh McPake, who play for Celtic and Hearts respectively, are all amongst the substitutes. This hopeful trio are all in line for their Scotland debuts if they enter the action later this afternoon.

Slovenski navijači se že zbirajo 👊🇸🇮#SrceBije 🇸🇮 pic.twitter.com/dM9UArGgl3

How much do the Tartan Army really know about new Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli? 🤔 We sent Jonathan Sutherland around Ljubljana to find out.📺 Watch 🇸🇮 Slovenia v Scotland 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 on Saturday on BBC One from 13:45 BST. pic.twitter.com/KSurjSmKwL

'We're not going to be perfect right away but we still demand results'Scotland's Lewis Ferguson as the team begins a new era under Sebastien Pocognoli 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿#BBCFootball pic.twitter.com/42WCJh66gc

Slovenia: Oblak, Brekalo, Bijol, Drkusic, Janza, Karnicnik, Cerin, Elsnik, Matko, Sturm, Sporar.

Subs: Vidovsek, Leban, Balkovec, Zabukovnik, Kuzmic, Begic, Lovric, Celar, Svetlin, Zec, Vipotnik, Horvat.

Scotland: Gunn, Hendry, McKenna, Welsh, Hickey, Gilmour, Ferguson, Robertson, McGinn, Ure, McBurnie.

Subs: Kelly, Bain, Binks, Doig, Christie, Miller, McPake, Doak, Graham, Bowie, Patterson, Montgomery.

On paper, it looks like Sebastien Pocognoli has opted for a five-back formation, with Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh making his Scotland debut as one of the centre backs.

Captain Andy Robertson and Brentford’s Aaron Hickey will operate as the wing-backs, with Billy Gilmour, Lewis Ferguson and John McGinn forming a midfield three.

A new-look attack is spearheaded by the returning Oli McBurnie and 22-year-old Robbie Ure, who like Welsh, will also make his Scotland debut.

Angus Gunn remains his country’s first-choice goalkeeper.

Sebastien Pocognoli's first Scotland XI to take on Slovenia 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿Watch the game live on BBC One Scotland from 13:45 BST 📺#BBCFootball pic.twitter.com/OnfWR7Gp8C

The squad's here 🏟️#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/IUiWhTHUT4

🚨 Znana je začetna enajsterica Slovenije za tekmo s Škotsko! 👊🇸🇮#SrceBije 🇸🇮 | #NationsLeague 🇪🇺 pic.twitter.com/rjEdMyyYGO

Debutants Robbie Ure and Stephen Welsh are each poised for their first international cap. Billy Gilmour returns to the starting XI after missing the World Cup through injury and Oli McBurnie will make his first appearance for Scotland since 2021.

Sébastien Pocognoli's first Scotland starting XI 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/JC6RGOq1QJ

“The first game is always a special game so you have to bring the mental aspect in for the players and for the staff.

“A good result can help but the most important thing is we see things that we work on through the week. I hope is we apply that well then we will get the result which will be the perfect mix.

“I hope we can bring a good game, and a good exciting principle on the pitch. I think we need the support from the supporters because there’s a lot of new players.

“We need to create a good energy but it’s up to us on the pitch to create this. So then we can be hand in hand with the supporters.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

Scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his new role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1424. Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Liam Drew is a freelance science journalist based near London.

Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (orange) can lead to changes in multiple nerve tracts.Credit: Nanditha Rajamani

Sixteen years ago, Simon Little was a junior neurologist thinking of devoting his time to international health work. But then he attended a lecture by Peter Brown.

Brown, a neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, UK, described his studies of people with Parkinson’s disease who had had electrodes implanted in their brains. The electrodes were intended to treat symptoms of this neurodegenerative disease by targeting electrical pulses to structures deep inside the brain. But to start with, Brown used them to record the oscillating waves of neuronal electricity that these brain structures emitted.

The recordings showed that as a person’s symptoms ebbed and flowed — their movements slowing then normalizing, their tremors flaring and subsiding — the oscillations changed1. “I was completely fascinated,” Little says. “The music of the brain was encoding something really powerful about people’s symptoms.”

After the lecture, Little asked Brown if he could do a PhD with him. Little laughs as he recalls how Brown tried to warn him off, saying that the field was a complete backwater and that Little would be pursuing this work at his own professional risk.

Undeterred, Little joined Brown’s laboratory, and the risk paid off. Little, now at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), and Brown took the signal most strongly related to the intensity of Parkinson’s symptoms — an oscillation in what’s termed the beta band, occurring 12–30 times per second — and used it as the trigger for deep brain stimulation (DBS).

Typically, DBS zaps the brain constantly. But by activating the device only when beta activity crested, Little and Brown could provide stimulation when a person most needed it. In an initial trial, numerical ratings of volunteers’ mobility were about 30% better than they were with constant stimulation2. “We found that less was more,” Little says.

Last year, the first ‘closed loop’ or adaptive DBS (aDBS) system for Parkinson’s, which operates similarly to the set-up that Little and Brown used in their early experiments, was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and earned a CE mark to be sold in the European Union. The technology — made by Medtronic in Minneapolis, Minnesota — uses the same electrodes to record beta-band activity and stimulate the brain.

Although this system is clinically effective, researchers think that it provides only a fraction of what smart implanted neurotechnologies could one day offer people with Parkinson’s. “This is a breakthrough,” says Wolf-Julian Neumann, a neuroscientist at Charité University Medicine in Berlin. “But it’s a super-tiny step towards the vision that we are pursuing.”

Neumann, Little and others say that emerging techniques and hardware now being tested in small clinical trials will lead to devices that decode, on the basis of neural activity, what someone with Parkinson’s is doing — say, sleeping, walking or speaking — and the exact symptoms they are experiencing. Then, with this real-time information, devices will deliver different forms of electrical stimulation to alleviate users’ symptoms and aid their movements3. “It’s a totally different way of conceptualizing the treatment of brain disorders,” says Neumann.

Parkinson’s disease is characterized by degeneration of the brain’s substantia nigra, a cluster of neurons that produces the neurotransmitter dopamine. This dopamine regulates the brain networks that coordinate voluntary movements. Without it, that system malfunctions.

“In Parkinson’s disease, you’ve got an unwanted brain arrhythmia,” says Helen Bronte-Stewart, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California. The extent to which neurons synchronize their firing at beta-band frequencies is abnormally high, producing a disruptive signal, she says. “It’s jamming the brain’s ability to coordinate movement.”

This leads to the hallmark symptoms of Parkinson’s: slowed movements, rigidity and tremors. The disease can also cause postural changes, speech difficulties and non-motor symptoms, such as depression or anxiety. In its later stages, cognitive decline is common. The standard treatment is to boost a person’s dopamine levels by dosing them with the drug levodopa. But levodopa can cause side effects, such as uncontrolled movements, and people can experience periods in which the drug’s effectiveness blinks on and off.

Since its clinical approval in 1997, DBS has emerged as a popular alternative for people whose Parkinson’s isn’t well controlled by drugs. Far and away the most common type of brain implant in use today, DBS has done much to normalize the process of undergoing neurosurgery to have a therapeutic device fitted. In its original form, the DBS electrodes — connected by wires that run down the recipient’s neck to a small power pack implanted in the chest — deliver a constant, high-frequency train of electrical pulses. Their target is either the subthalamic nucleus or the globus pallidus, two brain regions that are components of the movement network modulated by dopamine.

Simon Little (right) follows his patient Deb Zeyen as she demonstrates motor improvements.Credit: Yalonda M. James/Polaris/eyevine

Andreas Horn, a neuroscientist at the University of Cologne in Germany, says that ‘stimulation’ is a misnomer in DBS. The high-frequency zapping, he says, “is more about disrupting or overriding some circuitry that’s become dysfunctional”.

The change from continuous DBS to aDBS demanded that Medtronic incorporate the necessary technology into a compact medical device. Little says that in his first experiments, volunteers were wired up to racks of computers, filters and stimulators. Medtronic miniaturized that hardware so that it all fitted into the small implanted power pack.

Bronte-Stewart led the trial that secured the device’s approval4. This showed that aDBS was safe and that it controlled recipients’ symptoms effectively. The trial — somewhat controversially, Bronte-Stewart acknowledges — didn’t directly compare aDBS with conventional, continuous DBS. But just sending people on aDBS home and trusting they’d be safe was a groundbreaking step, she says.

Since 2020, Medtronic has been supplying a system capable of running either continuous or aDBS, and roughly 25,000 recipients could potentially switch to aDBS now. However, scientists are already taking note of the limitations of this system — and of using beta-band oscillations as a trigger.

One issue is that current aDBS systems take weeks of inpatient programming, with neurologists observing the effects of different sets of manually selected stimulation parameters5. “For this to scale, you can’t have every Parkinson’s patient needing three weeks of a neurologist monitoring them and optimizing this,” says Doris Wang, a neurosurgeon at UCSF.

Another issue is that beta oscillations provide only a crude indication of overall symptoms. “Beta power is essentially a biomarker of global worsening of symptoms of Parkinson’s disease,” says Neumann. Although this information is no doubt useful — not least, says Neumann, for effectively up- and downregulating DBS as levodopa’s effects change — beta-band oscillations don’t discern exactly what someone is experiencing. “Tremor actually reduces beta,” he says. As a result, “the beta-based adaptive DBS algorithm can confuse tremor for a good symptom state.”

What’s more, in current systems that use the same electrodes to stimulate the brain and record activity, artefacts from the stimulation compromise the quality of recorded signals6. Plus, these systems are recording from sites in the brain that are selected because they are best places to stimulate, and not necessarily the most informative to record from.

To address these issues and offer much finer control of the disease’s various manifestations, researchers are seeking to develop next-generation aDBS systems. On the input side, they are harnessing advances in brain–computer interfaces, including fresh technologies for recording and decoding brain activity. These, the researchers say, will be able to decipher exactly what users are doing and what symptoms are occurring.

On the output side, clinical studies are showing that it’s possible to halt symptoms of Parkinson’s by targeting separate neural pathways. For instance, Horn’s group has found that, by targeting adjacent but distinct nerve-fibre tracts (using conventional continuous stimulation), they can selectively help with tremor, rigidity, slow movement, or postural and gait-related problems7. “This is not so much about when to stimulate,” Horn says, “but rather about where and what to simulate.”

To map which nerve-fibre tracts passed close to the DBS electrodes, Horn’s team took brain scans of people who had had Medtronic devices implanted in the subthalamic nucleus. The scans showed tracts originating from different parts of the brain, such as the motor cortex or cerebellum, running near to the four contact sites on each electrode.

The researchers then stimulated various combinations of contact sites to steer currents to different chosen tracts. To their surprise, targeting specific fibre tracts ameliorated symptoms individually.

Horn and colleagues then developed an algorithm that, given a set of symptoms, will choose stimulation sites that should provide the most benefit. “If a patient has a lot of tremor, we tell the algorithm, ‘find me the stimulation volume that will maximally engage the tremor tract and not so much the other tracts’,” says Nanditha Rajamani, a neuroscientist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, who collaborated with Horn on this project.

In a small, five-person trial, the algorithm’s suggested settings produced a bigger improvement in the symptoms of four participants than did the stimulation their neurologists had previously set up for them7. The fifth person’s symptoms neither improved nor worsened.

Looking ahead, Horn says that because the manifestations of Parkinson’s shift constantly, the ability to target each symptom type could enable adaptive devices that suppress only the symptoms a person is currently dealing with. But that will require the device to ‘know’ what those symptoms are, meaning that researchers must identify the neural correlates of each symptom type.

To do so, they are recording brain activity while volunteers use wearable devices, such as accelerometers, to precisely track arm and leg movements. Increasingly, recordings are acquired not just from DBS electrodes deep in the brain, but also from a separate set of electrodes placed on the brain surface. These cortical electrodes pick up the signals that arise in the motor cortex to initiate and control movements. “There is a lot more information in the cerebral cortex,” Wang says.

Neumann’s group, for example, has used machine learning to link hundreds of features captured in such neural recordings to both symptoms and drug side effects. The features the researchers used correlated with symptoms better than beta activity did. And importantly, the model worked in people whose data had not been used to develop it.

Neumann thinks that this approach might even allow researchers to identify neural signals that precede symptoms. If so, future systems might not just react to symptoms as they occur, but could also pre-emptively stimulate the brain to prevent tremors and other typical manifestations of Parkinson’s from occurring at all. “When you and I intend to move, there’s a huge spike of dopamine release,” he notes. A well-timed burst of electrical stimulation could functionally substitute for this in people with Parkinson’s and thereby ease upcoming movements.

Neuroscientist Helen Bronte-Stewart assesses someone with Parkinson’s disease.Credit: Yalonda M. James/Polaris/eyevine

Neumann also thinks that if a smart DBS system can decode what a person is doing, or trying to do, this could help to select the stimulation activity that best serves that person. For instance, he says, the high-intensity stimulation that suppresses tremor can make it difficult to speak, so if brain signals indicate that a person is attempting to talk, then the tremor-suppressing stimulation might be turned down, or even off.

Likewise, Bronte-Stewart, Little and Wang are searching for neural correlates of movements and symptoms, with a view to controlling stimulation8. Little and Bronte-Stewart are also keen to treat symptoms of Parkinson’s that are not related to movement by finding appropriate signals and target structures to combat mood symptoms and cognitive difficulties, respectively9.

In June, Wang published a small trial that began to put the pieces together. It used movement-related brain signals to address a hugely problematic aspect of Parkinson’s: gait freezing, in which people who are walking suddenly become unable to move and so fall10.

After identifying cortical and subcortical signals that indicated the motions of walking, Wang’s group used them to trigger brief stimulation on the relevant side of the brain — the right side to affect the movement of the left leg, and vice versa. People who received this intervention fell less frequently than those who did not. “It’s the first demonstration that such rapid, movement-specific aDBS or closed-loop DBS is possible,” Wang says. Trial participants said that movement felt smoother and more fluid when using the system, and that it was easier for them to get up and walk.

It’s safe to say that Brown was wrong when he told Little that attempting to relate brain signals to disease symptoms was a dead end. But over the years, what it takes to bridge the gulf between exploratory research and a clinical product has become more apparent. “Our role as researchers is to show what’s possible,” Little says. Only then can the different questions regarding what can be scaled up into a viable clinical intervention begin to be addressed.

Already, there are questions about next-generation DBS that did not apply to the first adaptive systems. For instance, Little notes that if extra cortical recording electrodes are needed, surgeons will need to learn a new implantation procedure.

He is also wary of emerging systems being heavily dependent on artificial intelligence — either to decode brain activity or to get systems up and running without weeks of manual programming. Concerns swirl about embedding uninterpretable AI technology in medical devices, especially when people’s welfare and behaviour depend on it.

Little questions what would happen if someone using an AI-powered DBS system experienced a major mishap, such as freezing completely or crashing their car, because the algorithm changed its stimulation patterns. “Who bears responsibility for that?” Little says. This is an evolving space for both developers and regulators, who must find a sweet spot with which all parties are comfortable, he says.

The transformation of an idea into a clinical product is a balancing act between what’s possible and what’s plausible, reliable and safe. As Parkinson’s researchers aim to again lead the way in new forms of neurotechnology, they will need to navigate the known and unknown challenges that arise. As Bronte-Stewart says, today’s advances “are coming out of really good labs in academic centres doing a lot of computational work. How is that going to filter down into something that can be embedded in a system in your chest?”

#1423. England throw it away with defending unworthy of a top nation

There had been so much talk – first raised by Thomas Tuchel after the shocking World Cup exit to Argentina – about England’s DNA. About whether they could keep the ball, pass the ball, control the ball, the way Spain do.

The world and European champions were England’s first opponents – after the World Cup – in this Nations League campaign and came away from Wembley with a deserved win. They are now 39 games unbeaten with substitute Mikel Oyarzabal, who scored the winning goal against England in the final of the last European Championship, doing so again.

Mikel Oyarzabal SCORES against England AGAIN! 🎯Spain retake the lead after a slick finish from the Spaniard 👏#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pPT3KvRHWl

That may have been no surprise, even if the inevitable “olés” after Spain’s third goal will have hurt. But the nature of it? For the England manager this was another shocker. Not in the way his team went about the task. They were positive, fun, attacking. But in the way they conceded – goals and chances – and lost.

On this performance, DNA, for England, stands for Defensively Not Able, as they threw away what could have been a famous and restorative victory. Instead, with Croatia beating the Czech Republic in the other group game, England are under immediate pressure to win in Prague on Tuesday.

In fact, England have conceded 13 goals in their past six matches – in fairness including four in that third-place World Cup 6-4 win over France – and that is not good enough for a top-tier nation. Tuchel needs to sort it out defensively.

It could have been very different if Harry Kane had not missed from the penalty spot, slipping as he struck the ball, with England improbably 2-1 ahead. “It would have been the decisive punch,” Tuchel stated. Maybe so, even if there was always the feeling that Spain could go through the gears.

Kane MISSES from the penalty spot! 😧Harry Kane slips when he strikes the ball, let off for Spain and Luis de la Fuente#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pvg3GGa9ma

Afterwards there were claims, led by the impressive Anthony Gordon, that this was a missed opportunity for England. A bit like the World Cup. They need to shake this theme.

The irony was this was one of their best creative displays for quite some time. They took the game to Spain and could have scored more. And conceded more.

In truth it could have been Spain 4 England 0 inside half an hour and before Tuchel’s team laid a glove on their opponents.

Another let off for England 😧Ferran Torres misses another big chance one-on-one with James Trafford #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/KFkJoJUW6c

The manager had also spoken about how England should “embrace the chaos” as their best route to success. That may appear a questionable tactic – does chaos ever win a tournament? – but England certainly did that. This was as chaotic and, admittedly, entertaining as it gets.

England attacked with pace and power with the pick of their players the two based in Spain: Gordon, who scored, and Jude Bellingham. And the defenders? This was a bad night for Marc Guéhi, his Manchester City team-mate Nico O’Reilly (cue speculation about whether they were distracted by the verdict on the Premier League charges against their club) and for Jarell Quansah at right-back who is so evidently a centre-half.

A penny, once more, for the thoughts of the unused Trent Alexander-Arnold. The fourth defender, Ezri Konsa, vented his frustration at what was happening around him.

It was not just the errors but the unforced nature of them. Poor in possession with misplaced passes and defensively wide open. There is a gap between Spain and England but not as big as the gaps that were exposed in England’s back four. They endured a full house of calamities. They seemed strangely unaware – or incapable of dealing with – the danger posed by the outstanding Lamine Yamal.

Maybe because of the opposition – or the criticism – England felt the need to play out. But what an horrific start. What an inexplicable moment for Guéhi as he received the ball from O’Reilly and turned into trouble, gifting possession to Yamal who ran on and scored. Inside two minutes.

WHAT A START FROM SPAIN 🇪🇸Lamine Yamal pounces on a Marc Guéhi error to give Spain an early lead at Wembley #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/Et83EyTPlp

Spain walked out with the second star on their shirt – to mark their second World Cup triumph. That was the star Tuchel had promised for England.

Now, straight away, they were up against it. It could have turned very ugly. Ferran Torres, who had scored the winner in the World Cup Final, had one disallowed for offside, then was thwarted by James Trafford after – inexplicably again – being played onside by Quansah.

BIG SAVE from James Trafford 🧤The Leeds United goalkeeper keeps out Ferran Torres#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/nj5b8AUSQU

Then Torres was sent clear following Elliot Anderson’s poor pass, only to drag his shot wide. The third miss came from Dani Olmo, again set up by Yamal.

It could – it should – have been game over. Then England unexpectedly turned it around. They had kept attacking despite what was going on at the back and struck through a truly thrilling counter-attack, with Gordon and Bellingham combining before the Barcelona winger calmly beat goalkeeper Unai Simon.

ENGLAND ARE LEVEL! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿A brilliant finish from Anthony Gordon after a breathtaking counter attack 👏#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/z0nSfWIHVd

It was an exceptional goal and was quickly followed by a fortunate one as O’Reilly’s cross was met by Kane who stooped to steer in a header, only for it to strike Marc Cucurella, who made a mess of clearing, and it went past Simón.

I think we'll give that goal to Harry Kane 🎯England come from behind to lead Spain thanks Harry Kane, with assistance from Marc Cucurella ⚽️#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/X3qSOWUhVT

The Spain left-back hit the post with a cross, misjudged by Trafford who was given this game and the next to stake his claim ahead of Jordan Pickford who has so long been the undisputed first-choice.

England dominated for a while and Bellingham won a penalty, after a VAR intervention, only for Kane to strike the crossbar.

How Spain made them pay and worryingly so. O’Reilly passed the ball straight to Olmo who swept it inside. Substitute Álex Baena checked and beat Trafford from the edge of the area. Even worse was how Spain cut through the heart of England defence with Baena finding Oyarzabal. Why was no defender closer to him? What was Guéhi doing? And O’Reilly? Oyarzabal exquisitely dinked the ball over Trafford.

Thomas Tuchel does not think Manchester City’s guilty verdict over almost all of their Premier League charges distracted his England players in the Nations League defeat to Spain.

City players Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly were at fault for two of Spain’s goals and both Tuchel, the head coach, and England captain Harry Kane confirmed news of the verdict had been discussed among the squad.

Tuchel does not plan to address the issue with his players ahead of the remaining Nations League games against Czech Republic and Croatia.

Asked if the City verdict had been a cause of discussion ahead of the Spain game, Tuchel replied: “Not for me, but I can imagine maybe for the Man City players. I won’t comment on it as it’s an ongoing case.

“I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking about Spain and the team and meetings. The players have more time than me. So I can imagine they talk about it. It’s good they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”

Kane added: “There was a discussion, but when we’re with England, we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week.”

Tuchel also refused to point the finger of blame at Guéhi, O’Reilly or Kane, who missed a penalty, for England’s defeat despite admitting his team got off to the worst possible start by conceding a goal after two minutes.

“We will focus on the positives, but also highlight the stuff we can do better,” Tuchel said. “Not even speaking about individual mistakes because this is normal. It just happens. It should not happen, and for sure not in this amount. But there is no sense in showing the individual mistakes or telling them ‘please don’t make mistakes’. That is normal, but we can do things better. We can defend the third goal better. But we will focus on the positives. There is a lot to take away from the game.

“We wanted to be the team desperately to beat them [Spain] and we think we had them. We still think we had them at half-time. That was the way the team showed up after half-time. So we will focus on that, but the reality is we lost and the reality is we need to prove it again.”

“It was a terrible start, the worst possible start, which makes it so difficult against a team like this. The reaction was very good. After 10/12 minutes, we were the better team but we gave away too many mistakes. We were the better team. If we had converted the penalty, it could have been the decisive moment. We have to keep going and learn from the mistakes. We could have created more if we had been more clinical in the final 20 metres. We showed great bravery and courage with our high-ball wins. There will always be moments you suffer against teams like this. The effort and quality were there tonight but the result does not prove it today.”

“I think there is a gap [between Spain and England]. They [Spain] are the world champions and European champions. Mikel Oyarzabal was never going to miss. He was always in control of the situation. Honestly, people talk about sexy football, that is sexy football. I would watch that all night.”

🗣️ "We went toe to toe with the European and world champions" 💪Harry Kane remains positive about England performance despite their 3-2 defeat to Spain 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿🇪🇸#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/qkhqsqmPEl

🗣️ "You have to beat them to show people we can do this" 💪@IanWright0 reflects on England's 3-2 defeat to Spain at Wembley#ITVFootball | @markpougatch pic.twitter.com/ko2FYs4VqA

Marc Guehi and Nico O’Reilly may want to look away now but Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon scored well. Our very own Mike McGrath has provided his player ratings.

Tonight: England 2 Spain 3 (H)Tuesday September 29: Czech Republic (A), kick-off 7.45pmSaturday October 3: Croatia (A), kick-off 5pmTuesday October 6: Czech Republic (H), kick-off 7.45pm

🗣️ "I think it's a bit of a missed chance" 👀Anthony Gordon says mistakes cost England the win tonight against Spain at Wembley 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/AJBxVNjbjq

A highly entertaining game. England will probably argue the game changed on Kane’s missed penalty, but Spain missed a lot of very clear chances and will feel they deserved the victory. A losing start to the Nations League for Tuchel and his team, but there were some positives. Gordon, Bellingham and Anderson were all excellent. Some of the defending, not so excellent.

Possession: England 47%-53% SpainShots: 13-15Shots on target: 5-5Corners: 6-3Touches in opposition box: 37-15

England have one last chance with a corner out on the left. This will be it. Spain are able to deal with it and clear their lines.

Then comes the final whistle at Wembley and the world champions Spain claim a 3-2 victory in north London. It was an absorbing game, where momentum swung one way and then the other, but it is Spain who are the victors.

Baena brings down Rogers with a silly challenge to gift England a free-kick deep in the Spanish half. This could be England’s last chance.

Anderson is over it but his delivery is poor, easily caught by Unai Simon.

England are running out of time to find an equaliser.

O’Reilly appears to be suffering with cramp but England have made all five substitutions.

A late change for England as Branthwaite replaces Guehi.

Rogers delivers a dangerous cross from the right that runs through the six-yard box and forces Pubill to put it behind for a corner.

England take it short before Anderson clips it in but Laporte heads away.

Garner should have done so much better with that. His run into the Spain box on the left side is picked out by Anderson’s pass. Garner has Calvert-Lewin waiting at the back post but the former massively overhits the cross.

Double substitution from England as Calvert-Lewin and Gibbs-White replace Kane and Saka. Rare to say Kane taken off, especially when England are behind.

Saka goes down under a challenge from Cucurella inside the Spain penalty box but no penalty is forthcoming. VAR has cleared the incident. Moments later, Bellingham is then booked for stopping Spain going on the counter.

Spain make a change as Merino replaces Olmo.

The way Spain control possession and keep the ball is impressive. They toy with you pretty well and often look so composed.

Baena, who has been superb since coming on, feeds a lovely pass into the path of Oyarzabal on the right side of the box. Oyarzabal takes one touch before lifting it over Trafford into the England net. That is a lovely assist from Baena and lovely finish from Oyarzabal.

Mikel Oyarzabal SCORES against England AGAIN! 🎯Spain retake the lead after a slick finish from the Spaniard 👏#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pPT3KvRHWl

Given the quality of the opposition and the sustained threat he carried, that might have been Gordon’s best-ever performance in an England shirt. Him and Bellingham have been excellent. But now he’s been replaced by Morgan Rogers.

Guehi joins O’Reilly in the book for a cynical foul on Olmo. You can put that yellow card in the category of a professional foul.

England are making a double change as Garner and Rogers come on for Lewis-Skelly and Gordon. Garner was not in the initial squad but takes his chance now after the withdrawals.

Spain also make a substitution as Pedri replaces Ruiz.

At one end, Yamal has a shot blocked after England gave the ball away before Lewis-Skelly’s shot down the other end is easily saved.

The first booking of the night sees O’Reilly shown a yellow card for a foul on Yamal.

England come close to going back in front. After good work from Bellingham, Saka has it on the right side of the box. Saka cuts inside onto his left and looks to pick out the far corner but his effort goes narrowly wide.

Another big mistake from England is punished. It is absolutely dreadful from O’Reilly, who gives the ball away so poorly deep inside the England half. Spain capitalise and it is the man who has only just come on, Baena, who curls into the bottom corner from the edge of the box. All to play for with half an hour to go at Wembley.

SPAIN EQUALISE! 🇪🇸A brilliant finish from Alex Baena after a Nico O'Reilly mistake 🎯#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/tXygPfbPmb

Yamal and Baena exchange a lovely one-two on the right side of the box and you think the former will find the far corner but his effort goes wide.

How did Yamal MISS that! 🤯A big opportunity goes begging to pull Spain level! #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/jyzLm9VBd5

Cucurella has a real habit of making himself unpopular wherever he plays. The Wembley crowd have been booing his every touch and were not happy with him staying down after the ball hit him in the head. Spain haven’t got going at all in this second half.

Spain have made a double change as Oyarzabal and Baena replace Torres and Williams.

Kane steps up but his effort smashes into the bar. Kane slipped just as he took it. In fact, a free-kick is given to Spain as it was a double hit.

Kane MISSES from the penalty spot! 😧Harry Kane slips when he strikes the ball, let off for Spain and Luis de la Fuente#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pvg3GGa9ma

The referee overturns the original decision and points to the spot. A foul from a Barcelona midfielder on a Real Madrid midfielder is given.

Yet more England appeals for a penalty. Bellingham goes down, believing he was fouled by Rodri, but the referee gives nothing. There is contact but is it enough for a penalty? The referee had a good view and there is a decent shout for a penalty.

The referee is being sent to the screen so we know what that usually means...

Certainly no sitting on the lead from England at the start of the second half. Tuchel was adamant that Bellingham should have been awarded a penalty after going down in the area.

And Tuchel might get his way as VAR have sent referee Davide Massa to the screen.

England want a penalty. Saka goes down under a challenge from Laporte from behind but those appeals are waved away. VAR checks and clears the incident. Laporte got the ball.

Chance for England. Bellingham’s cross from the left picks out Quansah in the centre of the box but the defender’s header from eight yards out misses the target. What an opportunity that was for Quansah to score his first international goal.

Spain are unbeaten in nearly 40 competitive matches and, as it stands, that run is set to come to an end. Still a long way to come though tonight and Spain could have been 3-0 up before England even scored one goal.

We are back under way at Wembley. No changes for either side at the break.

During half-time, Kyle Walker received a framed shirt to celebrate his 96 England caps.

What a response from our #ThreeLions! 💪 pic.twitter.com/qBoY0J79JL

2 - Lamine Yamal has scored the third quickest goal England have ever conceded at Wembley Stadium, behind only first minute goals for Scotland in 1957 and Hungary in 1953.Punch. pic.twitter.com/NxVp1qOnVi

Possession: England 45%-55% SpainShots: 6-8Shots on target: 2-2Corners: 3-3Touches in opposition box: 10-10

Tuchel will be delighted with the half-time score and England’s spirit after going behind so early. But how on earth have Spain only scored once? They’ve missed a couple of one-on-ones, hit the post and blazed over the bar. Highly entertaining and England will know they will have to defend better if they are going to hold on to their lead.

An absorbing and end-to-end first half is brought to an end. Somehow, despite the fact at one point they could have been 3-0 down, England lead 2-1 at the break.

Cucurella’s cross from the left loops all the way to the back post, where it strikes the frame of the goal. I do not think Cucurella meant that.

It is chances galore at both ends, with the latest falling to Ruiz, whose shot from the edge of the box is deflected wide for a corner. Bellingham heads away at the front post.

England gift the ball away so poorly and Yamal should punish them with his second goal of the game but he blazes high over the bar.

What on earth has happened to Spain? O’Reilly’s cross from the byline picks out Kane, who guides a header towards goal. Cucurella makes an absolute mess of things, effectively kneeing the ball past his keeper and into his own net. Kane will try and claim it but surely that has to go down as an own goal. 10 minutes ago, Spain should have been 3-0 up. Now, England are 2-1 ahead.

I think we'll give that goal to Harry Kane 🎯England come from behind to lead Spain thanks Harry Kane, with assistance from Marc Cucurella ⚽️#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/X3qSOWUhVT

England are inches away from taking the lead. Saka drives forward towards the Spain box and lays it across to Kane, whose shot goes just wide. Should Kane have scored? Maybe.

SO CLOSE FROM KANE! 🫣England nearly go in front 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/YgoRblxuiH

Somehow, England are on level terms. Spain should have been 3-0 up but England equalise with a clinical counter-attack. Anderson wins the ball back for England on the edge of their own box and plays it forward to Gordon, who flicks it brilliantly first time into the path of Bellingham, who drives into the Spain half. Gordon is on his bike and is ready to receive the forward pass from Bellingham. Gordon takes it to the Spain box before slotting home clinically past Simon.

ENGLAND ARE LEVEL! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿A brilliant finish from Anthony Gordon after a breathtaking counter attack 👏#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/z0nSfWIHVd

England have missed Declan Rice’s delivery so far this evening. Saka has floated a couple of corners straight into the hands of Spain goalkeeper Simon and there have been some promising free-kicks wasted too.

No love lost between the Real Madrid team-mates Jude Bellingham and Marc Cucurella, there. Bellingham was unhappy with a challenge from the left-back and let’s just say they exchanged words afterwards.

If Olmo had slotted that home, the assist from Yamal would have been quite incredible. A quite sensational flick from Yamal plays Olmo in behind on the right side of the box and the latter’s shot goes narrowly wide of the far post.

Saka’s shot is blocked and the ball spins behind for an England corner out on the right. Saka takes the corner he won but his inswinger is caught by Unai Simon.

England want a penalty. Lewis-Skelly goes down inside the Spain penalty area under a challenge from Cubarsi and his appeals are waved away. The referee was spot on with that call.

That is a second sitter missed of the half from Torres and Spain should be 3-0 up. Rodri times his through ball to perfection and Torres’ first touch is glorious to take him past Anderson and away. Torres is one-on-one with Trafford and should score but his effort slides by the left post. How Spain are not 3-0 up is beyond me.

Another let off for England 😧Ferran Torres misses another big chance one-on-one with James Trafford #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/KFkJoJUW6c

That is a waste from Bellingham. The Real Madrid man is found by Quansah on the edge of the box and Bellingham should get his shot off quickly but dithers for too long. Bellingham then goes down far too softly, wanting a free-kick, but those appeals are rightly waved away.

England have enjoyed more of the possession thus far but are still yet to register a shot through 25 minutes.

The Spain fans are certainly enjoying their night in north London. In general, they have a lot to be happy about currently holding the World Cup and Euros trophies as well as the fact that their team is 1-0 up this evening.

That is a big save from Trafford and a big miss from Torres. Yamal plays a through ball to pick out the run of Torres, whom many in the ground think is offside. However, he was clearly being played onside by Quansah and Torres, who is fine scoring form this season for PSG, should score with a one-on-one opportunity but is denied by Trafford. England could and perhaps should be 2-0 down.

BIG SAVE from James Trafford 🧤The Leeds United goalkeeper keeps out Ferran Torres#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/nj5b8AUSQU

Anderson plays a lovely switch from right to left to pick out Gordon in space. Gordon takes just one touch before getting it out of his feet quickly, curling a cross to the back post. He is looking for Saka but Cucurella just about deals with it, even though he did not know much about it. The ball appeared to come off Cucurella last but a goal-kick is given.

After a very shaky start, England are beginning to grow into the game, slowly, but it is gradually happening.

England are really not helping themselves at the moment, gifting the ball away in dangerous area. This time it is Lewis-Skelly who gives it away and Spain end up with a corner.

The delivery is drilled to the edge of the box, where Yamal’s powerful volley is blocked by Gordon.

Spain keep it alive and the ball comes back into the England box. Torres fires into the bottom corner but the offside flag goes up and replays show he was clearly offside.

The OFFSIDE Flag saves England's blushes 👀Ferran Torres saw his close range finish chalked off #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/unIj6NsO7z

England have their first sight of the Spain goal. Kane plays Gordon in down the left and the latter gets past his man easily. He gets to the byline before crossing but Unai Simon in the Spain goal is on hand to cut it out.

What on earth are you doing Guehi? Spain take the lead inside two minutes and it is a real gift. Guehi should pass to O’Reilly or Gordon to his left but instead comes back towards his own goal, seemingly unaware that Yamal is right behind him. What then follows is a clinical finish from Yamal, who drives into the England box before curling towards the far corner, with the ball going in off the inside of the post. That will help Yamal’s pursuit of the Ballon d’Or. Dreadful from Guehi, fantastic from Yamal.

WHAT A START FROM SPAIN 🇪🇸Lamine Yamal pounces on a Marc Guéhi error to give Spain an early lead at Wembley #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/Et83EyTPlp

Now Tuchel is out with his arms crossed after that nightmare start from England. The Spain fans are in good voice.

We are under way at Wembley. There is VAR in use.

Tuchel was not shown on the big screens ahead of kick-off. He’s just got up off his seat for the first time and entered his technical area to complain about something.

Before we get under way at Wembley, we stop to remember the great Kevin Keegan with a minute’s applause, with a wreath being laid down on the side of the pitch. England are also wearing black armbands to remember Keegan. Wembley also pays tribute to a few other England players who have died over recent months.

England: Trafford, Quansah, Konsa, Guehi, O’Reilly, Anderson, Lewis-Skelly, Bellingham, Saka, Gordon, Kane.Substitutes: Pickford, Alexander-Arnold, Scott, Chalobah, Hall, Branthwaite, Rogers, Garner, Calvert-Lewin, Gibbs-White, Eze, Steele.

Spain: Unai, Pubill, Cubarsi, Laporte, Cucurella, Rodri, Ruiz, Olmo, Yamal, Williams, Torres.Substitutes: Raya, Martinez, Huijsen, Grimaldo, Merino, Lopez, Pino, Baena, Zubimendi, Pedri, Oyarzabal.

As feels customary at every England game, Oasis rings around the stadium to build up the atmosphere.

Here come the two sides and it is time for the national anthems. Marcha Real followed by God Save The King. There are plenty of Spanish supporters in attendance tonight and they are making their voices heard.

Here comes the Wonderwall compilation. Harry Kane said yesterday that he wants to win the Nations League next summer and then celebrate by going to one of the Oasis gigs.

Spain have been forced into a late alteration during the warm-ups and it comes at right-back, with Eric Garcia injured so Marc Pubill comes in.

I quite like Tuchel’s idea of giving Trafford the first two Nations League games, against Spain tonight and Czech Republic in Prague, and then going back to Pickford for the final two, in Croatia and against the Czechs at home. How will we ever know if England have an alternative to Pickford if nobody ever gets a proper go?

Chelsea’s Cole Palmer was one of a number of England withdrawals. Thomas Tuchel had his say on Palmer missing too many games in his press conference and ITV’s Roy Keane has had his say:

“If you think he is going to get England to another level, forget about it. I watched him before the break against Brentford. I think he has far too many bad habits for me.”

Harry Kane or Lamine Yamal? 🏆The ITV panel discuss some of the contenders to win the 2026 Ballon d'Or#ITVFootball | @markpougatch | @IanWright0 | @juanmata8 pic.twitter.com/bssBX0ljWF

Harry Kane wants England to address how they lost their identity and went “against our beliefs” at the World Cup.

In a brutally honest assessment of the tournament, the England captain admitted Thomas Tuchel’s team did not play to their full potential in several games – even before the painful semi-final exit against Argentina.

Kane, who played golf instead of watching the World Cup final, revealed the 2-1 Atlanta defeat hurt more than missing a penalty four years earlier in Qatar, when England were knocked out by France in the quarter-finals.

“This one hurt more than any other one. I would probably say even more than when I missed a penalty in Qatar because of the manner that it happened,” Kane said. “It was not us as a team.

“We trust our players and the player know very well that if you miss a camp then someone plays well in your position that the competition is always on. You have to make sure to be available and to produce top-level performances in camp and if you do so, that counts for something. Right now, it is not on my list of worries. I am not wired like this. From the moment I arrived at SGP my full focus is 100 per cent with the players who are here.

“There is no threat, distrust or threat of consequences. It will come naturally. I truly believe that we have the opposite. You will talk to our captain, Harry Kane, who has the most minutes for club and country and is happy to be here while teammates of his are enjoying a 10-day break. He is the role model and that is the vibe we have here.”

In memory of Kevin Keegan ❤️Today's official matchday programme ⤵️

James Trafford is poised to start for England ahead of Jordan Pickford against Spain tonight.

Pickford has been England’s No1 for eight years but Thomas Tuchel is set to make a change to face the world champions in the Nations League opener at Wembley.

Trafford went to the World Cup in the summer and has started the Premier League in good form following his move to Leeds.

In the first match since the World Cup, changing his goalkeeper is a major selection decision from Tuchel.

Elsewhere, Jarell Quansah is set to play at right-back ahead of Trent Alexander-Arnold while Myles Lewis-Skelly is also in line to return to the starting XI after being recalled into the squad after missing the World Cup.

England begin their Nations League campaign with a home game against the world champions Spain. This is England’s first game since the World Cup, with their dreams of glory ended by Argentina in the semi-finals, but they did finish third after beating France in a high-scoring third/fourth play-off. The last meeting between these sides saw Spain beat England to win Euro 2024. They also faced off in the Nations League back in 2018, with Spain winning at Wembley and England taking victory over in Spain.

England’s plans for these games has been disrupted by a number of withdrawals. Cole Palmer had earned a recall having been left out of the World Cup squad but the Chelsea forward has withdrawn due to a minor injury, despite playing the full game for Chelsea against Brentford in the final game before the international beak.

“He [Palmer] plays with discomfort and pain and cannot play on the highest level with discomfort and pain,” Tuchel said. “Chelsea informed us. That is my understanding. We are not managing load. This is not an ‘international break’. It is a competitive environment, where the players love to train and be together. That is what we created. We will never compromise on that. We will never let this feeling creep in that the players do not want to come [to England camps]. We focus on the guys who absolutely want to play for England.

“For sure it is a missed opportunity. It is another missed opportunity. He misses too many opportunities. I do not blame him for it, it is just a fact. He misses way too many camps with injuries. I only want to rely on what I personally witness and see within my team. For that you have to be in camp. If you are not in camp there is a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you can only do it with me on the pitch and with us on the pitch. It is a missed opportunity.”

Declan Rice has also withdrawn from the squad despite playing the full game in Arsenal’s defeat to Brighton as have Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento. Morgan Gibbs-White and James Garner have been called up as a result.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is back in the fold for the first time since June 2025. 18-year-old Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha made his England debut against New Zealand during the World Cup warm-ups and takes his place in this squad, although he does make the matchday squad for tonight’s game. England will also take on Czechia, Croatia and then Cezchia again during this international break.

Having been crowned world champions back in July, Spain are now champions of both Europe and the world. Back in June 2025, Spain made the Nations League final but lost on penalties to Portugal. Ahead of this international window, The Royal Spanish Federation has extended Luis de la Fuente’s contract until 2032. After tonight, Spain will host Croatia and Czechia before travelling to Croatia to cap off this international window.

This is an extended international break, with four games to take place during this window. Team news from Wembley to follow shortly.

#1422. Inside Oliver Glasner's Forest struggles: Unserious players who act like superstars when they don't deserve to, alarming physical data - and squad's grumbles revealed

Published: 12:00 EST, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 13:25 EST, 7 November 2026

If football management were gambling, Oliver Glasner has just done the equivalent of walking into one of Nottingham’s top casinos and chucking everything on red.

Not satisfied with hammering his Forest players publicly after Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at Brentford, Glasner then had the squad running on the banks of the River Trent for their customary Sunday recovery session. The social media footage has to be seen to be believed – Premier League footballers jogging through an overgrown field, filmed by a baffled dog-walker.

Even if Forest were doing well and their players were easy to manage, these would still be risky moves. Instead, Glasner's side are 19th in the table and he is trying to handle a notoriously restless dressing room.

Forest are believed to pay Glasner more than £10million a year and until now owner Evangelos Marinakis has been patient. But in the Premier League most fans are sceptical when club officials talk about long-term projects and three-year plans. Only three of the current 20 managers have lasted three years in their current job.

Any manager who loses regularly is under pressure, particularly at a club who sacked three managers last season and another in the summer. Glasner has lost six of 10 as Forest boss and won only once. Forget the spin: results alone mean Glasner is under the pump.

If there are no signs of a reaction against Manchester City on Saturday, it promises to be an uncomfortable November international break.

If there are no signs of a Nottingham Forest reaction against Man City on Saturday, it promises to be an uncomfortable November international break for Oliver Glasner

There was not one single moment that broke Glasner’s patience but the 30th minute at Brentford on Saturday probably contributed heavily.

Forest centre back Murillo, who has regressed alarmingly this season, watched idly as Bees goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher launched the ball way over his head and into the path of Dango Ouattara. Ouattara then breezed past Murillo before Nikola Milenkovic turned the cross into his own net. Glasner was unhappy with the shape Murillo was in when he returned for pre-season training and was furious at such slack work.

It was not the first time Forest had been exposed like this, either. Jay Dasilva’s winner for Coventry at the City Ground in September came from a similar diagonal pass from keeper Carl Rushworth, though that time Daniel Munoz – one of Glasner’s pupils – was at fault. Again, slack. Again, sloppy.

Daily Mail Sport understands Glasner does not see enough seriousness in his squad. This group of players get on well but nonetheless, there is a view that poor results do not hurt them enough. Is it really time for laughing and joking around the training ground when you have taken one point from a possible 15?

Most of this squad have never won a European trophy, or one in Europe’s top five leagues. Glasner has three. Some around him believe there are Forest players who carry themselves like superstars when they do not deserve to.

It is thought Glasner is also frustrated with himself. Looking back, perhaps he wishes he had started with a bang, because the 52-year-old was alarmed at the physical data from previous seasons.

In 2024-25, Forest covered fewer kilometres than any other team, and last season only Liverpool and Chelsea covered fewer. In 2024-25, only Arsenal made fewer sprints; last season, only Everton were below Forest. Glasner’s Palace sides were never lower than 12th in those four categories.

When Glasner has been outspoken in the past, it has usually worked. At Wolfsburg and Frankfurt, performances improved. At Crystal Palace last season, Glasner let rip at his bosses after a game at Sunderland last January and most expected him to be sacked. Instead, he left in the summer after delivering the Conference League. The dynamic at Forest is very different though – and Glasner may soon understand why.

Glasner was unhappy with the shape Murillo (left) was in when he returned for pre-season training and was furious at the Brazilian's slack work at Brentford

Player power was a major factor in Ange Postecoglou and Sean Dyche's sackings last season. When players believe they can go above the manager’s head and vent to those in charge, they will. This is the danger for Glasner.

Daily Mail Sport understands there are players who love neither the new style – Glasner is a committed three-at-the-back man and many of the squad feel more comfortable in a back-four – nor the Austrian’s strict approach. He is very different from the avuncular Vitor Pereira, whose easy charm and light-touch approach united the squad post-Dyche and kept Forest in the top flight.

Others are surprised Glasner has not made it a priority to bring the dressing room’s strongest characters onside. Along with Morgan Gibbs-White, both Ola Aina and Callum Hudson-Odoi are powerful voices in the squad and alienating any of them is dangerous. Equally, Ibrahim Sangare and Nico Dominguez are well-respected, and both have been left on the fringes like Aina and Hudson-Odoi.

While Gibbs-White is clearly Forest’s best player, he can be a complex character. If the skipper is not 'having’ a Forest manager, his position becomes vulnerable.

It was a turbulent summer for Gibbs-White, who was frustrated no Champions League club came in for him and ultimately changed agents. He was also left out of England’s World Cup squad. Some believe that Glasner’s rigid tactical framework does not bring the best from Gibbs-White, who likes to roam across the front line and drop deep when he wishes. While Pereira understood this, Glasner does not operate like that.

At times this season, Gibbs-White’s body language has been striking. Team-mates who make mistakes feel his anger but the 26-year-old has only one goal (a penalty) and two assists this term.

Gibbs-White watched team-mate Elliot Anderson leave Forest for City last summer and perhaps questioned why he was not on the same path to the Champions League.

It is tempting to wonder about some of the advice Gibbs-White has received from those around him, though. Because if Gibbs-White is wondering why he is still playing for a bottom-half Premier League club, it is never a bad idea to look in the mirror.

Callum Hudson-Odoi is a powerful voice in the dressing room and Glasner would do well not to isolate him

If  Morgan Gibbs-White is wondering why he is still playing for a bottom-half Premier League club, it is never a bad idea to look in the mirror

Marinakis did not make Glasner the highest-paid manager in Forest’s history just to show him the door at the first sign of trouble. When the pair held talks, Glasner is thought to have stressed the need for time to make his vision work.

Neither man suffers fools and it is easy to imagine that Marinakis would have approved of parts of Glasner’s outburst. That does not give Glasner a free pass, because Marinakis factored in player feeling when dismissing Postecoglou and Dyche.

If the Glasner experiment fails, George Syrianos will come under scrutiny. Forest’s chief football officer has more power at the club than at any other time and he pushed hard for Glasner, whom he has known for some time through links to German football.

It is believed the pair had some contact over possible transfer business during Glasner’s time at Palace, and Glasner would likely have welcomed the chance to work with Syrianos at Selhurst Park.

In December 2023, Syrianos wanted Glasner to replace Steve Cooper but Marinakis chose Nuno Espirito Santo instead. Marinakis’ son, Miltiadis, is at the training ground regularly and will report back to his father. These are testing times for Glasner and his champion.

Dyche has had his say, too. During a poor run of results last season, he gathered the Forest players and staff for their views on what needed to change.

Anticipating their opinions on formations and tactics, Dyche was bewildered when one player queried the decision to move the weekly barber visit from Friday to Thursday. Nevertheless, that player is still at Forest and Dyche lasted less than four months.

Dyche  made many mistakes at Forest but his latest posts on Threads felt relevant.

If the Glasner experiment fails, George Syrianos will come under scrutiny. Forest’s chief football officer has more power at the club than ever before and he pushed hard for Glasner

The problem at Forest is that even if the players fail to stand up and be counted, they are rarely the ones to pay the ultimate price

They read: ‘The badge is bigger than all… and yet it seems not nowadays! I can only hope it turns and the culture we were insisting upon is now being assessed and realised as what was and is needed. Oliver is out there saying what I was saying… in his own style.

‘Nottingham Forest are still finding the goals hard to come by – and I had it along with my staff – we scored but nowhere near what the metrics were telling us, so not enough to stay in our job?

'We had 35 efforts at goal v Wolves and yet a 0-0 result and it culminated in myself and staff being sacked. I hope Oliver is given more time, the fans stay with him and the players stand up and be counted.'

The problem at Forest is that even if the players fail to do so, they are rarely the ones to pay the ultimate price.

#1421. New Bromley boss Karl Robinson heaps praise on 'megastar' Jermain Defoe - with Premier League legend in talks over dugout return after walking out on Woking

Published: 08:00 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 13:33 EST, 7 November 2026

New Bromley boss Karl Robinson has hailed Premier League 'megastar' Jermain Defoe as the ultimate professional following his abrupt departure from Woking.

Daily Mail Sport revealed on Tuesday that Defoe is in talks to join Robinson's backroom staff at League One strugglers Bromley after Andy Woodman's dismissal last month.

And while his appointment has yet to be confirmed, Robinson jumped at the chance to wax lyrical about Defoe at his inauguration on Thursday.

Bromley sit bottom of League One but their new boss believes Defoe's meticulous attention to detail would help the players find another gear.

'There's been a lot of talk but there always is with names like Jermain Defoe, who is a megastar. He's one of the greatest Premier League strikers of all time,' Robinson said.

'I have to raise and change the narrative of what this stands for,' the new boss pointed to the Bromley badge on his jumper.

Jermain Defoe is in talks to join League One strugglers Bromley as Karl Robinson's assistant

Former Salford City manager Robinson has hailed 'megastar' Defoe as the ultimate professional

'I have to bring people in to make me the best version of myself. I spoke to people who know Jermain and played with him.

'He was always first in. All the players who have played with him will tell you that. Steven Gerrard will tell you that.

'He was first in and still in the training ground at 4pm - massages, recovery, gym, video analysis of the players he's playing against.

'I was speaking to him about something completely different the other day and we were talking about discipline and professionalism.

'I said to him: "what do you do that for?". He went: "If I do everything right Monday to Friday and I play poorly, I can accept it because I've done everything in the week to be the best version of myself."

'I'm listening and I've got goose pimples on my arm. Then I'm thinking, that's probably why you're Jermain Defoe, because he did everything he possibly could to maximise his talent.

Defoe has been out of work since walking away from National League side Woking after just four months at the helm amid a strained relationship with the club's director of football.

The 44-year-old took charge of the final six games of last season and was expected to lead the club into the new campaign.

However, he failed to report for work on the eve of the season before contacting the club later that day to inform them he would not be returning.

The former England international and Tottenham Hotspur striker would add top-level experience to the dressing room, having scored 163 Premier League goals in 496 appearances - ranking 10th on the Premier League's scoring charts.

Robinson spoke as though he idolised Defoe when quizzed on his potential appointment, highlighting his humility and relentlessness as key assets to succeed as a coach.

'Failure isn't falling short, it's when you don't maximise your talent. And I think some of the players here haven't maximised their athletic, technical and tactical capabilities', Robinson added.

'For whatever reason, we need to find the key to what that is. I think someone like Jermain (would bring that) because he maximised everything he was and everything he is.

'That's almost the secret behind the genius of the top players. It's their attention to detail, professionalism and discipline – he does that over and over again.

'He's tried to manage in non-league as well. That, in itself, is dropping your ego to learn.'

Although Bromley are still working on finalising Defoe's appointment, he is expected to join Robinson in the dugout at Hayes Lane. The Ravens host Rotherham in the first round of the FA Cup this weekend as Robinson takes his first game in charge.
